item.title: At the Moulin Rouge
item.lesson: Toulouse-Lautrec — aristocrat by birth, bohemian by choice, his growth stunted by a genetic disorder and two adolescent leg fractures — made Montmartre's nightlife his kingdom and painted it without glamour or judgment, from the inside. Here his actual circle sits around a table at the Moulin Rouge: critics, photographers, and performers he knew by name, with the dancer La Goulue fixing her hair in the background — and Lautrec himself crossing the rear of the room, a tiny bowler-hatted figure beside his towering cousin, his own height made into fact rather than tragedy. The picture's shock is the woman at right: her face lit acid-green by the room's new electric light, cropped by the frame like a snapshot gone wrong. At some point after his death the canvas was cut down — likely by a dealer who found that corner too strange to sell — and the severed strip was later reattached; the seam is still visible under close light. The strangeness was the point. Nobody painted modern nightlife's mixture of gaiety and ghostliness better, because nobody else lived at that exact table.
item.lookFor: The green-faced woman anchors the composition's genius: a diagonal balustrade rushing in from lower left, the table tipped up like a Cézanne, and electric light — brand new to the world — turning faces into masks.
